title: Anthropic ends Nasdaq debut 17% up, but Wall Street falls 2% and Asian chip stocks slide
dek: Shares of the Claude maker opened 34% above the IPO price before giving up half the gain, as the Dow closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. SoftBank fell 16% in Tokyo on Friday.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Shares of Anthropic, the US artificial intelligence company that makes the Claude models, closed their first day of trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $97.17, 17% above the $83 offer price, after opening at $111.50 and touching $114.99. But the record listing did not lift the wider market: the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,101.11 points, or 2.2%, to 49,097.06, its first close below 50,000 since June, and technology stocks across Asia fell sharply on Friday morning.

The S&P 500 lost 2.0% to 7,175.83 and the Nasdaq Composite 2.3% to 23,879.20, according to closing figures. Over the week so far the Dow is down 6.2% and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq about 5% each.

## The debut

Anthropic sold 980 million Class A shares at $83, raising about $81.3 billion, the largest initial public offering on record, the company said on Wednesday. The opening price was 34% above that. The stock then slid through the afternoon, to a low of about $92.72, according to reports, before recovering part of the loss by the close. It traded at about $92.60 after hours, one report said.

Reports differ on what the company is worth, because they count shares differently: about $1.3 trillion on shares outstanding at Thursday's close, or about $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis that includes employee options and other promised shares. Only about 7.4% of the company's shares are in public hands, according to one analysis cited in reports, which can make early trading in a new stock more volatile. More than half of the institutions that bid for shares received none, according to reports.

"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," chief executive Dario Amodei said, according to reports.

## Why the market fell

Analysts pointed to a rotation out of technology shares that began earlier in the month. Nvidia, the biggest maker of AI chips, hit a new 52-week low during the day after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sent the company an investigative subpoena over whether its advanced chips had reached China and whether it had misled investors about that risk, according to reports. Nvidia has been without a permanent chief executive since Jensen Huang stepped down on 12 November; chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive, the company said in a filing. AMD fell more than 6% after a short-seller disclosed a bet against it, according to reports.

"It all started with a big rotation out of tech," said Binky Chadha, chief strategist at Deutsche Bank, who described the market as "very oversold", according to reports.

## Asia on Friday

The selling spread to Asia when markets opened on Friday. SoftBank Group, which has invested $64.6 billion in Anthropic's rival OpenAI, fell 16.2% in Tokyo, on course for its worst day in more than two years, according to reports. Chip-equipment makers Tokyo Electron and Lasertec lost about 7% each. In Seoul, SK Hynix fell about 6%, Samsung Electronics 4.7% and the Kospi 3.7%. These are intraday figures and may change by the close.

## What it means for India

Indian shares rose on Thursday, with the Sensex up about 990 points as autos and banks led a rebound, but the selling abroad points to a weaker start on Friday: GIFT Nifty futures were trading about 0.5% lower in early trade, according to market data. Indian information technology companies, which earn most of their revenue in the US, are watched closely for signs that spending on AI is slowing or speeding up. The rupee closed at a provisional 93.36 to the dollar on Thursday, its fourth straight gain.

## What happens next

The Anthropic offering is due to close on Friday, and the underwriters have 30 days to buy up to 147 million more shares. Its first full week of trading, and US jobs and inflation data due in the coming weeks, will shape whether the slide in AI stocks deepens or eases.
